entries.title: Chris Van Hollen Is Challenging Chuck Schumer for Democratic Leader
entries.summary: The Maryland Democrat has been critical of Schumer, who has led the caucus for nearly a decade.
entries.content:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he would challenge Chuck Schumer for the top Democratic leadership role in the Senate, arguing the party needs to take a more populist direction.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, said in a statement obtained by The Washington Sun.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” he added. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Van Hollen, a favorite among progressives who is also considering a run for president, has been critical of Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, accusing them of siding with the cryptocurrency industry and American Israel Public Affairs Committee against progressive candidates.

Schumer said earlier this week that he is confident he already has more than enough support to be reelected leader.

“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues. We’re united,” Schumer told The Sun.

Schumer has faced sharp intraparty criticism over his past handling of government funding fights, with many Democratic voters blaming the longtime lawmaker for not doing more to stand up to President Donald Trump during his second term. Nearly all of the nine newly elected Senate Democrats set to take office in January have said they would not support him as leader, and several sitting Democratic senators have also called for new leadership.

Nevertheless, Schumer again expressed confidence that he will remain Democratic leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer said in a statement issued by his office on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together - 55 seats and counting is an amazing result- and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

On MS NOW on Thursday, Van Hollen said that he is running for leader because the midterm elections were a call to reform the political system more broadly and were not just a rejection of Trump.

“It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that's rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, and is fueled by a corrupt political system,” Van Hollen said. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Van Hollen said that he would tackle the first 100 days of a Democratic-led Congress differently from Schumer. Though he agreed with Schumer’s plans to reverse cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Van Hollen said that Democrats should expand their sights to reining in artificial intelligence and passing a higher federal minimum wage. 

He added that he would not have gotten involved in Democratic primaries as leader, after Schumer backed candidates in Maine and Michigan who ultimately failed to secure the party’s nomination. Van Hollen said more than 15 Senate Democrats have already pledged to support his bid for leader. 

“We should be focused on defeating Republicans, not getting involved,” Van Hollen said on MS NOW. “We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way. He supported establishment candidates in the primaries.”

Van Hollen also called on Democrats to reject donations from AIPAC. Schumer has faced criticism from the Democratic base for accepting donations from the group. 

“Some of the richest, most powerful people in the world are spending gobs of money in these elections to try to buy a Congress that will do their bidding,” Van Hollen said. “We need to get rid of super PACs. We need to get rid of secret money. We need to get rid of the Elon Musk loophole that allows him to try to buy a Congress while getting billions of dollars in federal contracts.”

The Democratic leadership elections aren’t expected to take place until early December, however, ensuring debate over the leadership race will drag on for several more weeks.

entries.title: The Commanders Keep Hope Alive With a Win Against the Giants
entries.summary: Stefon Diggs' late touchdown lifted Washington to a 24-21 victory in a "must-win" game.
entries.content:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Last week, in the moments after another frustrating loss, Jayden Daniels didn't hesitate in calling his team's Week 10 matchup with the Giants a "must-win." On Thursday night, the Commanders quarterback helped deliver that win as Washington squeaked out a 24-21 victory on the road.

After throwing two late interceptions — his first of the year — Daniels found a way to keep the Commanders' hopes for the season alive. Given one final offensive possession, he found receiver Stefon Diggs for a 32-yard touchdown with less than a minute remaining.

"When you get the opportunity to go win the game, you just take a deep breathe and go out there and capitalize on the moment," Daniels said.

The quarterback finished with 249 yards passing and three touchdowns as the Commanders moved to 3-5-1. They now sit just two games behind New York in the NFC East standings.

"We needed that," coach Dan Quinn said after the game. "We needed every bit of it, and I had a sense it would come down to the end."

The final drive came after linebacker Sonny Styles made a key tackle for loss on Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy on a third-and-3 with just under two minutes left. At that point in the night, after Daniels threw backbreaking interceptions on consecutive fourth-quarter possessions, it appeared Washington was headed for another deflating defeat.

"If you just be the player you are, the moment can never be too big," Styles said of the defensive stop. "I think everyone understood in that moment that we needed to get a stop right there."

After forcing the punt, Washington got the ball back with 1:49 remaining. Needing to go 71 yards for a touchdown, Daniels immediately threw a bomb to Treylon Burks, who drew a defensive pass interference for 33. Suddenly in business, a Washington offense that had struggled all night perked up. Daniels hit Diggs over the middle a few plays later, and the veteran wideout broke a tackle and slipped into the open field. Without no more defenders in sight, he waltzed into the end zone.

"[Daniels is] baby Kobe," Diggs said of his quarterback. "He does not flinch. He's going to be the same player at the beginning of the game as he is at the end of the game. Things are going to happen, good and bad — he is not going to change."

The Giants, needing a field goal to tie, mounted a drive of their own but it ended with Commanders corner Rasul Douglas intercepting a jump ball on third-and-long.

"I always think I'm going to make the play," Douglas said. "When the ball is in the air, I don't ever really see the receiver. I just know I'm going to get it. ... Some guys play the man — that's not me. I want interceptions, I want the ball."

It was not the prettiest of victories for Washington. Overall, the offense still looked stagnant, punting on four of its first seven drives. The defense was up and down, limiting New York to seven points in the first half but giving up big plays in key moments. Early in the fourth quarter, the Giants took a 21-17 lead on a 66-yard touchdown by tight end Isaiah Likely. Styles and K’Lavon Chaisson ran into each other in coverage, allowing Likely to break free and sprint to the end zone.

But Washington didn't quit on the game, and the team will head back to D.C. with a key win in hand. The Commanders welcome the surging Bengals to Northwest Stadium for "Monday Night Football" on Nov. 23.
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: A Tragedy in Logan Circle
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Nov. 12, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A firsthand account of the lead-up to a shooting that left one dead and shook a vibrant D.C. neighborhood. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 3/10. Gray, gusty and suddenly November. After weeks of warmth, it’s time to bundle up. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Late last year, Matt Lambert reached out to The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler with a story pitch: his million-dollar Logan Circle penthouse had been rendered unlivable.

In a firsthand account, Brice-Saddler — who worked for The Washington Post at the time — recalls visiting Lambert at his home and listening to the doctor describe how a dispute over severe water leaks and black mold had turned into “psychological warfare” between himself, building manager James Stuart, the management company EJF Real Estate Services and their insurance defense attorneys.

“It’s affected every part of my life — my sleep, dietary habits,” Lambert said. “I pride myself on my resilience, and I’ve been kind of surprised at how much it has been affected.”

On Thursday morning, the dispute came to a violent end when Lambert killed Stuart and shot four others at and near VIDA Fitness Gym on his condo building’s ground floor.

The Sun’s Metro team reports that police were on scene within 30 seconds of receiving the first report of the shooting, which came in just before 8 a.m. After tending to victims and evacuating the building, they found Lambert in his seventh-floor penthouse and spoke with him for about an hour, during which time he fired at officers at least twice through the door. Police forced their way into the apartment after hearing a gunshot inside and found Lambert dead with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

According to an online profile, Stuart, 46, had worked for EJF for more than a decade.

“We’re devastated,” Mayor Muriel Bowser said at a press conference. “Someone was killed in our city this morning. A senseless act of gun violence.”

The streets of Logan Circle, a vibrant neighborhood that has long served as a social hub and the home base of the District’s LGBTQ+ community, went eerily silent in the aftermath of the shooting. By Thursday afternoon, police confirmed that much of the conversation between Lambert and police centered on his dispute over building conditions. In addition to three firearms — a shotgun, a rifle and a handgun — police found containers of gasoline and other flammable materials inside his apartment.

Four victims were taken to local hospitals. Three of them have non-life-threatening injuries, and the fourth remained in critical condition Thursday.

On Thursday evening, Joel Braithwaite, who represented Lambert in the litigation, said his client had been in high spirits in the days prior to the shooting, having started a new job.

“Dr. Matt Lambert was an emergency room physician, someone that was in the business of healing people,” he said. “Litigation wears on you, and it takes a toll on people, and some of the tolls are not necessarily visible.”

At one point during a tour of his apartment last year, Lambert pointed to a copy of Sun Tzu’s “The Art of War” sitting in his stripped-down unit.

“I go through every emotion every day on this,” he told Michael. “Do I keep fighting? Do I not fight? And ‘The Art of War’ talks about, you know, the battle’s won before it’s ever fought. It says if you’re going to commit, don’t half commit, fully commit.”
Shooting Vida 15th st nw 003 (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)





FROM THE DISTRICT

A Way-no, for now. D.C.’s transportation committee has voted down a bill that would have legalized passenger service in self-driving cars operated by Waymo and other companies, stalling a nearly 15-year effort to bring this technology to the District, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. Though the legislation is dead for now, Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George told The Sun that she is pro-AV and is committed to convening agencies to take up the issue again when she is in office.

D.C. Council chambers were packed Thursday for a hearing on what At-Large council member Elissa Silverman called the District’s “house on fire”: truancy. Nearly 40% of D.C. public school students were identified aschronically absent last year, with family obligations, safety concerns and mental health challenges cited as potential causes. The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports that witnesses praised some current mitigation strategies, including the District’spilot truancy-reduction program, but agreed that more needs to be done.

One student who walks his younger sister to school said he often faces an “impossible” decision: “wait for a delayed bus, or complete a 20-minute walk to get her to school, just to still risk being marked absent or tardy.”

The staff of Washingtonian magazine has unanimously voted to authorize a one-day strike after five years of contract negotiations with management. Staffers say it’s a “last resort” needed to “cross the finish line,” The Sun’s Nicole Belcastro reports.





SPORTS

Commanders 24, Giants 21. In a game that Jayden Daniels labeled a “must-win,” the Commanders delivered. Stefon Diggs’ caught a 32-yard touchdown with less than a minute remaining and the Commanders kept hope alive with a much-needed divisional win. Daniels finished with 249 yards passing, three touchdowns and two interceptions as Washington moved to 3-5-1. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down the players and the plays that delivered a victory.

It will be a busy Saturday afternoon at Audi Field this weekend, as the much-discussed scheduling conflict between the Spirit’s NWSL semifinal and the Division III Secretaries’ Cup football game was resolved Thursday in surprising fashion. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports that the soccer game will begin at noon, as planned, and the football game will kick off at 4:30 p.m. To pull off the tight doubleheader, stadium officials plan to paint the field with NWSL lines in yellow and NCAA yard lines in white.

There’s a lot to be excited about at Capitol One Arena this year: The revamped Wizards are looking to level up and Alex Ovechkin is savoring a farewell tour. But The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that fans on social media have focused at least some of their attention away from the action, to where new luxury seats have proved to be an eyesore at games.

The Lexus Vault seats, connected to high-end suites that the stadium opened last year, have consistently sat empty as patrons enjoy other amenities away from the court or ice. “It became a conversation … just because of how glaringly empty they were,” one fan said. “It looks like there’s a giant empty section.”

What to Watch This Weekend

Friday

NCAAM: Georgetown at Clemson, 6 p.m. (ESPNU)

NCAAM: Maryland vs. Virginia, 8 p.m. (Peacock)

Saturday

NWSL: Spirit vs. Utah Royals, noon (CBS)

NCAAF: Maryland vs. Wisconsin, noon (FS1)

NHL: Capitals vs. Devils, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

Sunday

NCAAW: Maryland vs. Columbia, 1 p.m. (B1G+)

NBA: Wizards vs. Rockets, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Commanders Heartthrob Sam Hartman Is the Next ‘Bachelor’
entries.summary: Fans of “The Bachelor” appear to be thrilled about the selection.
entries.content:
Sam Hartman, a quarterback in the Washington Commanders organization, will serve as the next “Bachelor” on the eponymous reality dating show, ABC announced on Friday.

Hartman, 27, will star in the show’s 30th season, in which roughly 25 women will compete for his heart.

Hartman was on the Commanders' active roster until August, when he was cut. He was quickly re-signed to the team’s practice squad, where he continues to play.

The former Notre Dame standout spoke about his decision to join the show in an interview with “Good Morning America” on Friday.

He said he’s excited about the opportunity to find the love of his life but is nervous about the experience.

“I have probably a tough time holding a conversation with one girl,” he said. “Thirty is going to be pretty tough.”

Hartman said his teammates gave him dating advice for the show, but he declined to share their comments on the air.

His parents told him to be himself and enjoy the experience, he said.

Hartman said he’s looking for a compassionate person and not necessarily someone who can catch a football.

As a 2024 undrafted free agent, Hartman spent the past two seasons switching between the team’s practice squad and the active roster.

“Bachelor” fans were thrilled about the selection.

“And just like that Bachelor is SO back,” one commenter wrote on social media.

Another person wrote: “I will get on a flight right now!”

Hartman, a Charlotte, North Carolina native, is 6’1 and weighs 209 lbs, according to his Commanders profile.

entries.title: Senate Republicans May Fall Short Confirming New Trump Foot Soldiers
entries.summary: The clock is ticking fast, many nominees are stuck in committee and some GOP senators just have other priorities.
entries.content:
One top goal Senate Majority Leader John Thune declared this week is to confirm “a whole lot of” loyal White House nominees to bolster the administration before a combative Democrat Congress begins. Key senators say it's going to be a heavy lift.

Advancing judges who serve lifetime appointments has long been a high-profile goal of both parties, and Republicans have introduced and voted on a record number. But the second administration of President Donald Trump has leaned especially hard into asserting its executive power and has counted on loyal upper- and mid-level foot soldiers to carry out marching orders, even when they’ve violated previous norms and expectations and wound up in court battles.

But the supply of such people will run dry once Democrats hold 55 or 56 seats in the Senate.

The good news for Thune and company is there are a lot of would-be officials on deck: around 160 civilian, non-judicial nominees are awaiting a Senate vote. Also, Republicans have changed Senate rules to allow administration nominees to be confirmed in batches on the floor, making final votes easier.

The bad news for them is many of the outstanding executive nominations are still sitting in committees.

A count by The Washington Sun found that more than 130 administration candidates are awaiting hearings or votes on the relevant panels, while only around 30 have been reported to the floor. That means committee leaders will have to get as many hearings and votes as possible on the books in just a few weeks if Trump is going to get his officials.

Some chairs, such as Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), who leads the Environment and Public Works Committee, told The Sun that is exactly her plan.

“We’ll get them out and then up to the floor into the tranche,” Capito said. “I think that's what a lot of other people are trying to do.”

But some of her colleagues were more skeptical. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee has the biggest backlog of nominees, with more than 50 ambassadors and other roles awaiting action.

There are 23 pending State Department positions alone, including nominations for ambassadors to Hungary, Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates and the director of the Peace Corps.

Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho), the Foreign Relations chair, told The Sun that he didn’t want to comment offhand about whether the committee would be able to move those nominations before January, but said it’s “a legitimate question.”

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, echoed Risch, adding that he anticipates some of the executive nominations may take a backseat to more pressing issues in the final weeks of a Republican Senate.

His committee has fewer positions to review –– among them an assistant secretary of defense and an assistant secretary to the Navy –– but Wicker noted that he has more important priorities to contend with.

“It’s going to be difficult,” Wicker said. “The legislative votes, to me, are more significant than nominations for positions that come and go … My goals for the 50-plus days we have left in this year include the NDAA [National Defense Authorization Act] and some vehicle to fund national defense adequately."

Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas), though, told The Sun he feels confident that he will be able to move remaining executive nominations out of the Senate Agriculture Committee during his final weeks as chair.

Boozman said Agriculture is different because most of the nominees “shouldn’t be partisan.” Boozman added that he has worked closely with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), the top Democrat on the committee, to advance nominees who will help farmers around the country.

“We've got a really good chance of getting them out of committee,” Boozman said. “It is challenging, but because we’re working together on the committee, there’s no delay tactics or anything like that. So I think we’ll be ready.”

But, some of the other executive appointees sitting on committee calendars are more controversial with Democrats — and even some Republicans — than Boozman’s nominees might be.

For instance, Lindsey Halligan, who is tabbed to be the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, previously worked as a personal lawyer and later an aide for Trump. She has no previous experience as a prosecutor.

Catherine Eschbach, who was nominated as the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s general counsel, received a hearing on Tuesday but has still not been confirmed by the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. She was previously a corporate lawyer for SpaceX and oversaw efforts to downsize the EEOC and carry out the president’s goal of ending diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

Another nominee who could face Democratic pushback is Gary Lawkowski, who has advised the president on pardons and is nominated to become the top lawyer at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. A hearing on the nomination is scheduled for next week.

And Michael LoSapio, nominated to fill the long-vacant job of director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has also faced pushback from Democrats because of his current position at Palantir. The company received pushback after its data analytics and artificial intelligence software was used for government surveillance, military action and aggressive immigration enforcement.

Another roadblock is Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota), who has put holds on “any and all” Trump nominees while the administration continues to reject his demands to change a wetland conservation program that farmers in his state oppose.

Holds do not stop nominees from moving forward entirely but slow down confirmation. Cramer has agreed to release some nominees, and a White House official told the Washington Examiner on Thursday that conversations with Cramer are progressing.

Considering all the competing priorities and numerous impediments to moving nominees, though, it is likely that some of them will never get through.

And Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) told The Sun that even if the Senate were to stay in session until every single executive nominee were confirmed, he doesn’t think a focus on Trump officials would be a good use of time.

Instead, Republicans should be working with Democrats to find areas of common ground to benefit voters –– especially after such a resounding election, Justice said. “Of course” voters won't remember the GOP working around the clock to confirm more Trump administration appointees, he added.

“We’re going to say, ‘Well, we’re going to work night and day.’ But who’s going to remember that?” Justice said. “Two years from today, are the voters going to sit around and say, ‘Well, I’m going to vote for Republicans because they stayed in there on Saturday and Sunday.’ No.”

entries.title: Trump Allies Are Looking for a Shield From the Supreme Court
entries.summary: As congressional Democrats prepare to investigate, White House official Peter Navarro wants the justices to make it harder to convict for contempt of Congress.
entries.content:
Trump allies are hoping the Supreme Court will help shield administration members from a wave of subpoenas once Democrats take control of Congress.

Peter Navarro, a senior White House official, has asked the Supreme Court to overturn his convictions for contempt of Congress related to the last Trump administration. He was convicted for not complying with requests for information from the House panel investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

Navarro wants the justices to throw out a decades-old precedent and make it harder for prosecutors to prove administration officials defied a congressional subpoena, an outcome his attorney says could “even the playing field” of oversight powers between Congress and the executive branch.

Navarro is being represented in part by the America First Legal Foundation, which was co-founded by new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. Among those urging the Supreme Court to take up the petition are the America First Policy Institute think tank and The Article III Project, a Republican-aligned group that says it fights judicial corruption and “leftist lawfare.”

“Just one more reason why my appeal at the Supreme Court is so important,” Navarro posted Wednesday on social media about Democratic plans for oversight. In another post he said: “If they can come for me, they can come for you.”

Josh Hammer, senior counsel for Article III, said separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches will be a major issue in the next two years, adding that administration officials caught between orders from the president and responding to a subpoena from congressional Democrats would be “between a rock and a hard place.”

"It seems they want to at least threaten subpoenaing and investigating not just your top-line Cabinet officials, but level-B and level-C employees,” Hammer said. “A lot of these folks are definitely going to be looking at this petition, just to gauge and assess what that could mean for themselves."

Also backing the petition is Jeffrey Clark, a former DOJ official who floated a plan to challenge the 2020 presidential election results and who returned to the second Trump administration but has since left for the Oversight Project.

“If the Court settles the rule now, before the subpoena tsunami, the next fights over Stephen Miller or anyone else go where the Constitution sends them: negotiation and accommodation, and if that fails, a civil case. Not a grand jury,” Clark posted on social media Tuesday.

In an interview, Clark said he worries an unfavorable outcome from the court could embolden Democrats, including likely House Judiciary Committee Chair Jamie Raskin. The Trump-aligned Justice Department would be unlikely to prosecute executive branch officials for failing to respond to Democratic subpoenas.

Even if Democrats can’t get a conviction for contempt of Congress while Trump is in office, they have five years before the statute of limitations for refusal to testify runs out. A favorable opinion from the Supreme Court could further shield administration officials if a Democrat were to win the presidency in 2028.

“They’re harassing people who worked in the executive branch,” Clark said of potential Democrat-led subpoenas. “Then trying to get them to slip up or get information to come out that they can use and hand off to a Democratic-led Justice Department to do prosecutions.”

Clark was subpoenaed and appeared before the Jan. 6 committee twice; both times, he declined to cooperate during testimony.

Navarro served four months in prison in 2024 after a grand jury found him guilty of refusing to testify and produce documents for the Jan. 6 panel. He argued that he was limited from defending himself on a good-faith mistaken belief that executive privilege had been asserted, meaning he was shielded from subpoenas.

His petition asks the justices to hear his appeal, which centers on the word “willfully” in the contempt of Congress law.

“High-ranking officials should not have to worry about going to jail for a good-faith belief that executive privilege prohibited them from complying with a congressional subpoena,” his petition says.

The federal appeals court in Washington smacked down that “purported good-faith defense” in a July ruling that upheld Navarro’s conviction, pointing out that the Supreme Court has repeatedly reaffirmed a nearly century-old decision on that question.

“For the record, Dr. Navarro has not argued to this court that he ever had a good faith belief that the subpoenaed materials he created as a private citizen, published to the world, and spoke about publicly were subject to executive privilege,” the ruling says.

The Justice Department withdrew from prosecuting Navarro’s appeal almost a year before that ruling without explanation. But Navarro’s appeal to the Supreme Court is against the Justice Department, which has until Dec. 9 to file a response to his petition.

The Supreme Court did not rule on the same issue in an previous appeal from Steve Bannon, a former senior White House official, who was also convicted for not complying with subpoenas from the Jan. 6 committee and served four months in prison.

Instead, the Justice Department at that time said it was seeking to vacate Bannon’s conviction in lower courts, and the justices sent the case back down without a ruling.

Abhishek Kambli, Navarro’s attorney, said he thinks a favorable decision from the Supreme Court in Navarro’s case could “take down the temperature” on threats of investigations because it could take criminal prosecutions off the table in the future.

“What ended up happening in the Jan. 6 era was very quick-trigger — to send things to the DOJ for prosecution for contempt of Congress,” Kambli told The Washington Sun. “This would force more back-and-forth in negotiation between Congress and the witness before exercising the nuclear option of indicting and prosecuting someone.”

Democrats won a majority of both chambers of Congress in the midterms, giving them control of committee subpoena power. On election night, Sen. Robert Garcia (D-California) posted on X: “LAWYER UP.”

Rep. Bennie Thompson, the chairman of the now-defunct Jan. 6 committee, dismissed Navarro’s argument.

“The Trump administration is using every tool it has to attack congressional oversight, and Peter Navarro is going so far as to ask the Supreme Court to rewrite history,” Thompson said in a written statement.

“The Supreme Court needs to decide whether it will uphold longstanding precedent and Federal law or side with the lame-duck occupant of the White House, who is fast losing his influence and his already tenuous grip on reality,” Thompson said.
